## ✅ What actually matters today

  *What happened:* GAIL (India) reported a 139.3% year-on-year surge in consolidated net profit to ₹4,720 crore for Q2 FY27, alongside a 32.7% rise in operating revenue [[Economic Times]](https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/markets/ipos/fpos/gail-q2-results-profit-zooms-139-yoy-to-rs-4720-crore-revenue-rises-33-board-approves-gail-gas-ipo/articleshow/135356210.cms). *Why it happened:* Strong operational performance and robust demand propelled earnings, prompting the board to approve an initial public offering for subsidiary GAIL Gas Ltd. *Why it matters:* It highlights solid momentum in India's state-owned energy sector despite broader macroeconomic headwinds. *Who is affected:* Energy investors, public sector bondholders, and retail gas consumers. *What happens next:* GAIL Gas will file draft prospectus papers with SEBI for a domestic market listing.

## 🔍 Truth check
- **Claim:** A viral video circulating on social media claims that citizens in Tel Aviv, Israel, gathered at the beach to chant the *Hanuman Chalisa* in Hebrew to honor Indian pilot Smith Machar for rescuing passengers from a Dubai flight [[FACTLY]](https://factly.in/telugu-viral-video-showing-israelis-singing-hanuman-chalisa-in-tel-aviv-was-created-with-ai/).
- **Verdict:** ❌ **False** [[FACTLY]](https://factly.in/telugu-viral-video-showing-israelis-singing-hanuman-chalisa-in-tel-aviv-was-created-with-ai/)

## 🎓 Today's lesson
**What is a P/E Ratio (Price-to-Earnings Ratio)?**
The P/E ratio is one of the most popular metrics investors use to determine whether a stock is overvalued or undervalued. It is calculated by dividing a company's current stock price by its earnings per share (EPS). For example, if a company's stock trades at ₹1,000 and it earns ₹50 per share over the past year, its P/E ratio is 20. This means investors are willing to pay ₹20 for every ₹1 of the company's current earnings. A high P/E ratio usually implies that investors expect rapid future growth, while a low P/E ratio can indicate a mature company or a stock that is out of favor. However, comparing P/E ratios only makes sense within the same industry, as tech companies often trade at much higher multiples than traditional banks or utilities.
